name: Maya Chen
title: Senior Research Fellow
biography: Maya studies neutron stars through long-baseline pulsar timing, with particular attention to timing noise, rotational changes, and compact-object behaviour. She analyses pulse arrival times from MeerKAT and Murriyang using TEMPO2, PSRCHIVE, Python, time-series methods, and carefully constructed ephemerides. Maya is a useful person to consult when a project needs pulsar-timing strategy, interpretation of subtle timing residuals, or advice on turning repeated radio observations into a robust physical measurement.

name: Daniel Brooks
title: Research Fellow
biography: Daniel investigates how ionised material between stars changes the brightness, arrival time, and frequency structure of observed pulsar signals. He works with MeerKAT, Murriyang, and ATCA dynamic spectra, applying scintillation analysis and signal-processing workflows in PSRCHIVE, DSPSR, and Python. Daniel is well suited to consultations about unexpected pulse variability, dispersion or scintillation effects, and separating propagation signatures from intrinsic behaviour in radio time-series data.

name: Priya Nair
title: Lecturer
biography: Priya models compact-object populations and investigates how radio-transient observations constrain neutron-star formation and evolution. She combines ASKAP and MeerKAT samples with Bayesian inference, population modelling, and statistical classification implemented in Bilby, Stan, and Python. Priya can help when a study needs principled uncertainty estimates, comparison of competing population hypotheses, or a careful treatment of selection effects while connecting individual transient detections to broader astrophysical populations.

name: Elias Hart
title: Instrument Scientist
biography: Elias develops calibration strategies for radio receivers and studies instrumental systematics that limit sensitive interferometric and single-dish observations. He characterises noise and receiver response on ASKAP, ATCA, and MeerKAT using interferometric calibration, CASA, Miriad, Python, and controlled diagnostic measurements. Elias is a practical contact for planning radio calibration, diagnosing suspicious amplitude or phase behaviour, and deciding whether an apparent astronomical feature could instead arise from the instrument or observing setup.

name: Sofia Alvarez
title: Research Fellow
biography: Sofia studies how neutron-star and pulsar populations are born, evolve, and become visible to high-energy and radio surveys. She uses Murriyang and Fermi survey constraints with population synthesis, Monte Carlo modelling, and survey simulations built in PsrPopPy, Python, and R. Sofia is useful for questions about pulsar demographics, survey selection effects, population statistics, or whether an observed sample can reliably represent the underlying compact-object population.

name: Aisha Rahman
title: Postdoctoral Researcher
biography: Aisha searches wide-field radio observations for fast radio bursts and uses their dispersion and positions to investigate distant matter and host environments. She develops dedispersion, transient-detection, and radio-localisation workflows for ASKAP, CHIME, and MeerKAT data using PRESTO, HEIMDALL, and Python. Aisha is a strong contact for designing burst searches, validating impulsive candidates, interpreting dispersion measures, or planning the observations needed to localise a fast radio transient.

name: Thomas Vale
title: Senior Lecturer
biography: Thomas develops rapid optical-transient pipelines for discovering variable and explosive sources in repeated wide-field imaging. He applies image differencing, light-curve analysis, and alert filtering to Vera C. Rubin Observatory and ZTF data with the LSST Science Pipelines, Astropy, and Python. Thomas can advise on handling large alert streams, distinguishing genuine variability from imaging artefacts, and building efficient follow-up criteria for time-sensitive optical discoveries.

name: Keira Morgan
title: Research Fellow
biography: Keira studies supernovae and other stellar explosions by combining optical spectra with the way their brightness changes over time. She uses VLT and Gemini South observations for spectral classification and light-curve fitting, working with SNID, IRAF, and Python to examine diagnostic spectral lines. Keira is useful when a transient needs classification, when spectra must be connected to an explosion history, or when an observing programme needs guidance on supernova follow-up and cadence.

name: Luca Bennett
title: Lecturer
biography: Luca studies gamma-ray-burst afterglows across X-ray, optical, and radio wavelengths to understand relativistic jets and energetic explosions. He combines Swift, Fermi, and ATCA observations through afterglow modelling, spectral-energy-distribution fitting, and X-ray spectroscopy in XSPEC, HEASoft, and Python. Luca can help interpret multi-wavelength fading behaviour, construct a physically consistent afterglow model, or identify which follow-up observations would best constrain a high-energy transient.

name: Nadia Okafor
title: Research Fellow
biography: Nadia coordinates rapid searches for electromagnetic counterparts to gravitational-wave, neutrino, and other time-critical astrophysical alerts. She cross-matches IceCube and LIGO notices with Vera C. Rubin Observatory data, organising follow-up through GCN and analysing candidate lists with TOPCAT and Python. Nadia is an appropriate contact when teams need an alert-response plan, cross-facility coordination, candidate prioritisation, or a reproducible way to connect messenger events with observations across the sky.

name: Helena Park
title: Associate Professor
biography: Helena studies how galaxies assemble their stars, enrich their gas, and change over cosmic time through their integrated light. She combines deep JWST, VLT, and Hubble spectroscopy with stellar-population synthesis and spectral-energy-distribution fitting in Prospector, pPXF, and Python. Helena is useful for interpreting galaxy spectra, reconstructing star-formation histories, assessing chemical enrichment, or selecting observations and models for a galaxy-evolution project.

name: Marcus Ilyin
title: Research Fellow
biography: Marcus searches for high-redshift galaxies and measures their structures to investigate how early systems formed during cosmic dawn. He analyses deep JWST and Hubble infrared imaging with photometry, image decomposition, and gravitational-lens modelling in GALFIT, Lenstronomy, and Python. Marcus can advise on finding distant-galaxy candidates, using strong lensing to reach fainter sources, separating blended morphology, or designing measurements that remain reliable near an imaging survey's detection limits.

name: Rina Das
title: Senior Lecturer
biography: Rina investigates how supermassive black holes accrete matter and influence their host galaxies through active galactic nuclei. She combines Chandra and XMM-Newton X-ray spectroscopy with VLT emission-line analysis, using XSPEC, pPXF, and Python for spectral fitting and physical diagnostics. Rina is a valuable contact for classifying possible AGN, interpreting emission lines or X-ray components, and separating black-hole activity from stellar processes in galaxy observations.

name: Oscar Webb
title: Research Fellow
biography: Oscar maps neutral hydrogen in and around galaxies to understand gas accretion, feedback, and the environments that regulate star formation. He builds 21-centimetre spectral-line images from ASKAP, MeerKAT, and ATCA interferometry, using CASA, SoFiA, and Miriad for calibration, imaging, and source finding. Oscar can help with HI survey design, radio data cubes, reliable gas-source catalogues, or interpreting how a galaxy's atomic-gas reservoir relates to its evolution.

name: Yuna Patel
title: Lecturer
biography: Yuna uses large cosmological simulations to connect the growth of dark-matter structure with observable galaxy formation and large-scale structure. She runs N-body and hydrodynamic calculations on national high-performance-computing facilities, analysing SWIFT and HDF5 outputs with Python and comparing simulated populations with Gaia-informed constraints. Yuna is useful for simulation design, scalable analysis of large model volumes, interpreting dark-matter effects, or translating theoretical predictions into quantities an observational survey can test.

name: Amara Singh
title: Senior Research Fellow
biography: Amara estimates the physical properties and population characteristics of merging black holes and neutron stars from gravitational-wave signals. She applies Bayesian parameter estimation and signal inference to LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA observations using Bilby, LALSuite, and Python, with careful attention to posterior uncertainty. Amara can advise on compact-merger inference, prior choices, interpreting correlated parameters, or combining individual detections into a defensible population analysis.

name: Felix Rowan
title: Research Fellow
biography: Felix develops analytic gravitational-wave models for inspiralling black holes and neutron stars, focusing on binary dynamics and tests of general relativity. He uses perturbation theory, model validation, Mathematica, LALSuite, and Python to compare predicted waveforms with simulations and the needs of LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA analyses. Felix is useful when a project needs waveform selection, approximation-error assessment, physical interpretation of inspiral structure, or a bridge between relativistic theory and data analysis.

name: Chloe Mensah
title: Lecturer
biography: Chloe simulates colliding black holes and neutron stars to predict the gravitational and electromagnetic signatures produced by compact-object mergers. She uses finite-difference methods and the Einstein Toolkit with C++ and Python on national high-performance-computing systems, connecting numerical-relativity outputs to LIGO observations. Chloe can help formulate merger simulations, assess numerical accuracy, interpret remnant behaviour, or determine which simulated signatures are most relevant to multi-messenger measurements.

name: Samuel Ito
title: Instrument Scientist
biography: Samuel characterises noise and data quality in gravitational-wave detectors so weak astrophysical signals can be distinguished from instrumental artefacts. He applies time-frequency analysis, noise-spectrum studies, and continuous monitoring to LIGO and KAGRA data with GWpy, LALSuite, and Python. Samuel is the right person to consult about detector glitches, suspicious transient features, data-quality vetoes, or determining whether an analysis is limited by the instrument rather than the astrophysical model.

name: Leila Costa
title: Postdoctoral Researcher
biography: Leila combines gravitational-wave measurements with gamma-ray and optical observations to study binary-neutron-star mergers and their kilonovae. She performs joint Bayesian inference, parameter estimation, and light-curve modelling with LIGO, Swift, and VLT data using Bilby, MOSFiT, and Python. Leila can help connect multiple messengers within one analysis, interpret kilonova brightness and colour evolution, or identify which follow-up observations most strongly constrain neutron-star merger physics.

name: Ava Lind
title: Senior Lecturer
biography: Ava measures the composition and temperature structure of exoplanet atmospheres using the changing spectra seen during planetary transits and eclipses. She applies atmospheric retrieval and radiative-transfer modelling to JWST, Hubble, and VLT observations with petitRADTRANS, TauREx, and Python, including careful treatment of molecular signatures. Ava is useful for planning transmission-spectroscopy programmes, testing possible atmospheric compositions, evaluating biosignature claims, or understanding degeneracies and uncertainty in an exoplanet spectrum.

name: Noah Kwan
title: Research Fellow
biography: Noah determines stellar chemical abundances and ages to trace the formation and enrichment history of the Milky Way. He analyses high-resolution spectra from the VLT and AAT alongside Gaia information, using spectral synthesis and abundance workflows in MOOG, iSpec, and Python. Noah can advise on stellar-spectrum quality, robust element measurements, connecting chemistry with Galactic populations, or designing a galactic-archaeology sample that avoids misleading observational biases.

name: Farah Wilson
title: Lecturer
biography: Farah uses subtle, periodic brightness variations to probe the internal structures, evolutionary states, and ages of stars. She performs frequency and time-series analysis on TESS and Kepler light curves, then compares observed oscillations with stellar models built through Lightkurve, MESA, and Python. Farah is a helpful contact for detecting stellar oscillations, interpreting power spectra, distinguishing variability mechanisms, or combining asteroseismic constraints with a broader stellar-evolution investigation.

name: Benicio Torres
title: Research Fellow
biography: Benicio maps cold molecular clouds to understand how turbulence, dense gas, magnetic environments, and feedback shape the formation of new stars. He uses ALMA, Mopra, and ATCA molecular-line observations with radio interferometry and cloud-segmentation workflows in CASA, Astrodendro, and Python. Benicio can help select gas tracers, interpret complex data cubes, identify meaningful cloud structures, or connect protostellar activity with the surrounding interstellar medium.

name: Grace Kim
title: Senior Research Fellow
biography: Grace models the long-term orbital evolution and stability of planetary systems, including interactions that produce resonances and transit-timing variations. She combines TESS, Gaia, and Kepler constraints with orbit integration and dynamical stability tests in REBOUND, Mercury, and Python. Grace is useful for interpreting unusual transit times, testing whether a proposed planetary architecture is stable, identifying orbital resonances, or planning follow-up measurements that distinguish between competing dynamical explanations.

name: Ibrahim Clarke
title: Associate Professor
biography: Ibrahim develops statistical methods for astronomical datasets that are uncertain, incomplete, heterogeneous, or shaped by complex survey selection. He uses Bayesian hierarchical modelling, model comparison, and uncertainty quantification in Stan, R, and Python, with applications to Gaia and Vera C. Rubin Observatory samples. Ibrahim can help formulate a defensible probabilistic model, diagnose selection bias, compare competing explanations, or propagate measurement uncertainty through a population-level scientific conclusion.

name: Zoe Marin
title: Research Software Engineer
biography: Zoe builds reproducible scientific workflows for astronomy teams processing large datasets across shared, cloud, and high-performance-computing systems. She combines workflow engineering, automated testing, and parallel computing with Nextflow, Astropy, and Python to make data pipelines traceable and repeatable. Zoe is a practical contact when an analysis must scale beyond a laptop, when collaborators need consistent environments and provenance, or when a fragile research script needs to become a reliable maintained workflow.

name: Julian Adeyemi
title: Lecturer
biography: Julian applies interpretable machine learning to classify variable sources and discover unusual objects in large time-domain and survey datasets. He develops classification, anomaly-detection, and feature-engineering methods for Vera C. Rubin Observatory and ASKAP data using PyTorch, scikit-learn, and Python. Julian can advise on training-set design, model evaluation, explainable classifications, rare-object searches, or deciding when machine learning is appropriate for an astronomical source-catalogue problem.

name: Mei Foster
title: Research Data Specialist
biography: Mei helps researchers discover, query, and combine astronomical archives through interoperable metadata and virtual-observatory standards. She works with Gaia and the ESO Science Archive, using catalogue cross-matching, ADQL, TAP services, TOPCAT, and Aladin to turn distributed holdings into usable research datasets. Mei is useful when a project needs an efficient archive-search strategy, reproducible catalogue joins, metadata guidance, or help diagnosing why records from different services do not align cleanly.

name: Theo Grant
title: Research Fellow
biography: Theo designs visual analyses for multidimensional astronomical catalogues and studies how uncertainty can be communicated without obscuring the underlying evidence. He combines Gaia and TESS data through catalogue cross-matching, exploratory analysis, and uncertainty visualisation using Python, TOPCAT, and D3.js. Theo can help when a team needs to reveal structure in a complex dataset, build an interactive scientific graphic, compare linked catalogues, or present uncertain results clearly to specialist and broader audiences.
